etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English behaven, bihabben (“to restrain, behave”), from Old English behabban (“to surround, embrace, hold, contain, hold back, withhold, restrain”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihabbjan, equivalent to be- +‎ have. Cognate with Middle Low German behebben, behāven (“to receive, acquire, reach, keep”), Low German behebben (“to act, behave”), German behaben (“to behave”).

definitions.definition: (reflexive) To conduct (oneself) well, or in a given way; to conform.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Maccabees 2:21:
quote.text: And the manifest signs that came from heaven unto those that behaved themselves manfully to their honour for Judaism […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To act, conduct oneself in a specific manner; used with an adverbial of manner.

quote.citation: 2014 April 21, “Subtle effects”, in The Economist, volume 411, number 8884:
quote.text: Manganism has been known about since the 19th century, when miners exposed to ores containing manganese, a silvery metal, began to totter, slur their speech and behave like someone inebriated.

quote.citation: c. 1605–1608, William Shakespeare, “The Life of Tymon of Athens”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene v], page 88:
quote.text: He did behave his anger ere 'twas spent.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, The Faerie Queene, book 2, canto 3, verse 40:
quote.text: But who his limbs with labours, and his mind / Behaues with cares, cannot so easie mis.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To act in a polite or proper way.

quote.citation: 2009, Roger L. Van Ommeren, From Rebellion to Submission, page 48:
quote.text: One time when Willie was more set on clowning than on learning about Jesus, Miss Helen ordered, "Willie Mack, you stand up against the wall until you learn to behave."
